paper.title: Occupations and Import Competition: Evidence from Denmark
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed in the article. …

registers.name_in_paper: Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
registers.years: 1996-2008 (analysis window; high-quality ISCO occupation codes available from 1991)
registers.role: sample frame; worker-level outcomes (income, occupation, employment status) and worker characteristics; worker-firm linkage
variables_mentioned: unique personal identifier assigned at age 15

registers.role: firm-side information used to build occupation-sector histories and the sector aggregation; linkage to trade data

registers.years: approximately 1995-2007 for the exposure measure; 1995-2005 for the price indices
registers.role: treatment construction: import penetration at industry and occupation level, and industry-level import price indices
variables_mentioned: annual quantities of imports and exports by firms at the product-country level
annual values of imports and exports by firms at the product-country level

registers.role: construction of industry-level foreign (import) price indices by the Broda and Weinstein (2006) method; Danish custom codes mapped to industries using Prodcom
variables_mentioned: import quantities by product and partner country

registers.name_in_paper: Danish national accounts, published by Statistics Denmark
registers.role: calibration of the demand side: consumer demand coefficients, input-output matrix, capital input coefficients, capital income (gross surplus), export demand shifters and industry TFP

registers.name_in_paper: O*NET database (US Department of Labor survey of working activities)
registers.role: construction of occupational task vectors (ten principal components of ~130 survey items) used in the switching-cost function and in the Mahalanobis task distance
variables_mentioned: importance rankings of predetermined work activities on a 1-5 scale

linkages: Workers linked to a unique employer identifier within IDA (“it links employed workers to a unique employer identifier”, p. 4263).
IDA linked to the Firm Accounting Statistics Register (FIRE) to construct occupation-sector histories for each worker; “the match rate between employed workers and firms is nearly perfect” (p. 4263).
UHDI linked to FIRE, allowing import penetration measures at both the industry and the occupation level (p. 4263).
US 6-digit SOC occupations in O*NET mapped to the 38 author-defined occupation-sector pairs (online Appendix D).

sample.universe: Danish residents in IDA, followed as workers older than 23 and below 65, 1996 through 2008
sample.unit_of_observation: worker-year (income and employment measured each November); for the second-stage regression, cells defined by occupation-triple career arcs (o, o', o'') crossed with worker states (skill, unobserved type, age grid, occupational tenure) and years
selection_rules: Restrict to workers older than 23 and below 65 (p. 4263).
Restrict to the years 1996 through 2008, avoiding the first years of the ISCO-coded data and the 1994 labour-market reforms (p. 4263).
Drop observations whose occupation Statistics Denmark flags as imputed from education, industry and income, to avoid circularity in regressing income on occupations (pp. 4263-4264).
Drop observations with income in the bottom and top 2.5 percent to remove outliers (p. 4264).
sample.n_observations: 18.2 million worker-year observations from an underlying sample of 32 million

construction_notes: Occupations defined at the ISCO two-digit level; the army (code 01) and legislators (code 11) are dropped and managerial occupations (codes 12 and 13) are combined, leaving 22 two-digit codes (footnote 4, p. 4264).

Workers grouped into four sectors by industry: manufacturing (including utilities and construction, NACE 1 2-digit 0-45), FIRE and R&D (NACE 1 2-digit 64-74), health and education / public services (NACE 1 2-digit 75, 80, 85-90), and other services; after cleaning there are 38 occupation-sector pairs (pp. 4264, 4267).

Three skill groups from highest completed education: high school completion or less; short cycle (two years of vocational training); professional bachelor's (medium cycle) or more (ISCED 5-6) (p. 4263).
Tasks: ten principal components of ~130 O*NET work-activity survey items, explaining over 80 percent of the variation in survey responses (p. 4265).
Task distance between occupation-sector pairs is the Mahalanobis distance d((o,s),(o',s')) = sqrt((v_{o,s} - v_{o',s'})' Sigma^{-1} (v_{o,s} - v_{o',s'})) (footnote 9, p. 4265).
Occupational exposure to imports, equation (1): exposure_o = sum_{j in Inds} (L_{ojt-1}/L_{ot-1}) x (Delta Imp_{sj}/L_{jt-1}); all weights calculated in the base year (p. 4269, Figure 4 note).
Import values normalized by the 2000 Danish CPI (Figure 4 note, p. 4270).

Industry import price indices built from Danish customs unit values by the method of Broda and Weinstein (2006); Danish custom codes mapped to industries using Prodcom; the aggregate index is presented relative to the Danish CPI (Figure 6 note, p. 4293).
Changes in the price of commodities related to energy (coke and petroleum) are shut down in the counterfactual (footnote 44, p. 4292).
Discount factor fixed at beta = 0.96; it is “only tenuously identified in dynamic discrete choice models” (p. 4276).
Two unobserved types per skill level, i.e. six types in total; log(theta) for type 6 (college-educated, high absolute advantage) normalised to 0 in every occupation (pp. 4277, 4282).
Standard errors in Table 5 are block bootstrapped: parentheses block by individual (re-estimating both stages); brackets block over time periods in the second stage only (p. 4280, Table 5 note).

Counterfactual simulation: 100,000 individuals drawn from the empirical distribution of workers alive at the incidence of the trade shock (calendar year 1996), simulated under the equilibrium with and without the observed changes in import prices, with the same shocks used in both simulations; earnings discounted at beta = 0.96 (footnote 49 and Table 9 note, pp. 4296-4297).

claims.statement: In column (1): full model with specific human capital, occupations and demographic controls, the estimated switching elasticity parameter 1/rho — the coefficient on the income differential in the transition equation (17) — is 1.428.

treatment.label: Income (skill price times expected human capital) differential between the destination and the origin occupation-triple

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research): worker income and occupation, measured each November, linked to firms via the Firm Accounting Statistics Register (FIRE) for the sector dimension. No Statistics Denmark variable codes are printed.

definition.value: The right-hand-side regressor of equation (17): (1/rho)(w_{o't} E_varsigma H_{o'}(omega, varsigma) - w_{ot} E_varsigma H_o(omega, varsigma)), i.e. the difference between the expected real income a worker with state omega would earn in the destination occupation-triple o' and in the origin occupation-triple o. Skill prices w_{ot} and the human capital function H_o(omega, varsigma) (including returns to occupational tenure, age and unobserved comparative advantage theta) come from the first-stage income regression. In columns (2)-(4) the human capital terms are suppressed and incumbent wages are used instead.

timing.value: Measured between consecutive Novembers, t and t+1, over 1996-2008; the worker's state omega is measured at the beginning of period t, before the choice.

outcome.label: Log relative transition rate between occupation-triples

register_source.value: IDA: occupation (ISCO two-digit) and employment status each November, linked to FIRE for the NACE 1.1 industry/sector. No Statistics Denmark variable codes are printed.

definition.value: The left-hand side of equation (17): log[pi_t(omega, o, o')/pi_t(omega, o, o)] + beta log[pi_{t+1}(omega', o', o'')/pi_{t+1}(omega'', o, o'')], built from nonparametrically estimated first-stage transition probabilities for cells of workers with the same observed state and unobserved type. Transitions are measured between consecutive Novembers.

timing.value: Transition rates between consecutive Novembers t to t+1 and t+1 to t+2, pooled over 1996-2008 (T = 12).

units.value: coefficient 1/rho: the semi-elasticity of the log relative transition rate with respect to the income differential, in units of years of income (equivalently, the inverse of the scale rho of the Gumbel switching-cost shocks)

magnitude.interpretation: The paper reads 1/rho as the elasticity of switching occupations with respect to income shocks: for column (1), “The estimated value of 1/rho is 1.43”, which implies a mean elasticity of exit of -1.33 and a 4.4 percentage point rise in the exit rate from a permanent 1 percent income decline (pp. 4283-4284).

estimand.target_population: All Danish workers in the model economy: the parameter is common to every worker in the estimation sample (workers older than 23 and below 65, 1996-2008).
estimand.time_horizon: Annual decision period; the parameter is assumed constant over 1996-2008 (in column (5) switching costs are allowed to vary over time).

population.description: Danish workers older than 23 and below 65, 1996-2008, from IDA linked to FIRE; imputed-occupation observations and the top and bottom 2.5 percent of the income distribution dropped. 18.2 million worker-year observations from an underlying sample of 32 million.
subgroups_defined: three skill groups (high school or less; short cycle / vocational; professional bachelor's or more)
two unobserved comparative-advantage types within each skill group (six types)
population.selection: Conditioning on being an employed or non-employed Danish resident aged 24-64 with a non-imputed occupation code and income between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles; immigrants are more likely to be dropped because their education is often missing (footnote 3, p. 4264).

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in observed transition rates across career arcs (o, o', o'') among workers with identical observed characteristics and unobserved type who begin and end in the same occupation-triple but make different intervening choices (finite dependence), combined with variation in estimated occupation-sector skill prices over 1996-2008. There is no external shock or reform: identification comes from the structure of the dynamic discrete choice model.

key_assumptions.assumption: The t+1 forecast errors in the estimating equation are uncorrelated over time and with contemporaneous variables at time t (so the realized transition rate can replace the expectation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test. The author notes that zeta may also reflect shocks to eta, which must then be unanticipated and i.i.d. over time, and cites Kalouptsidi, Scott, and Souza-Rodrigues (2018) on the difficulty of identification and of finding good instruments (footnote 23, p. 4279).

key_assumptions.assumption: Assumption 1 (Information Sets): the worker knows the full set of skill prices at time t when choosing an occupation-triple; idiosyncratic productivity shocks are unknown at the time decisions are made and revealed only upon employment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix H relaxes the timing assumption in two directions (wage shocks observed; neither wage shocks nor skill prices observed); the author reports “Neither assumption significantly changes my estimates” (p. 4280).

key_assumptions.assumption: Assumption 2 (Conditional Independence and GEV(1) Errors): conditional on the state, the switching-cost shocks are i.i.d. across occupation-triples, individuals and time, Gumbel distributed.
Assumption 4 (Human Capital Accumulation): human capital is nontransferable across occupation-triples; tenure increments by one when the worker stays and resets to zero when the worker switches.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix F estimates an alternative model with sector- as well as occupation-specific human capital; the author reports the magnitudes of the returns to occupational tenure are robust (pp. 4274, 4281).

formal.as_written: ten_{it+1} = ten_it + 1 if o_{it-1} = o_it; 0 if o_{it-1} != o_it

key_assumptions.assumption: Finite dependence / renewal: two workers who are identical at t-1 and both switch into a new occupation at t+1 are again in the same state at t+2, regardless of any intervening career decision, so the initial and final continuation values difference out.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows from Assumption 4 by construction; no separate empirical test is offered.

formal.as_written: T(T(omega, o, o), o, o') = T(T(omega, o, o'), o', o'')

key_assumptions.assumption: The discount factor is not identified and is fixed at beta = 0.96.

Finite mixture: unobserved comparative advantage theta is drawn at the start of a career from a distribution with finite support, with two unobserved types per skill group (six types in all), and a combination of workers whose collective transitions span the set of occupations identifies the full vector of productivity shifters.

threats_discussed: Workers may have more or less information than assumed, making observed equilibrium skill prices a noisy measure of forecasted skill prices; Dickstein and Morales (2018) show measurement error can lead to large and ambiguously signed biases in nonlinear models (p. 4280).
If human capital is partially transferable, equation (17) is misspecified and both left- and right-hand-side variables carry nonclassical measurement error (p. 4281).

Serially correlated unobservable aggregate preference shocks (shocks to eta) would violate the forecast-error assumption; identification is difficult and good instruments hard to find (footnote 23, p. 4279).

Residuals combine first-stage measurement error in transition probabilities and workers' forecast errors, so one should ideally cluster over both individuals and time, which is infeasible here (p. 4280).
The panel is short (T = 12): few time clusters for the bootstrap and possible small-sample bias (p. 4280).
Tenure effects may reflect learning about comparative advantage or within-occupation firm upgrading rather than human capital accumulation (p. 4281).
robustness_checks: Two sets of block-bootstrapped standard errors: blocks by individual (re-estimating both stages) and blocks over time periods in the second stage (p. 4280).

Online Appendix G: a sqrt(N)-consistent estimator based on Altuğ and Miller (1998); “This changes point-estimates slightly, but 1/rho and the parameters governing costs all remain significant” (p. 4280).
Online Appendix B.9: the split-sample bias correction of Dhaene and Jochmans (2015); “The bias is small, but not insignificant” (p. 4280).

Online Appendix H: alternative timing assumptions (wage shocks observed, as in Dix-Carneiro 2014; and neither wage shocks nor skill prices observed) — “Neither assumption significantly changes my estimates” (p. 4280).
Online Appendix F: an alternative model with sector- as well as occupation-specific human capital (p. 4281).
Online Appendices F and G report 1/rho in (1.4, 2.2) across variants (footnote 36, p. 4286).
unresolved_confounders: Whether tenure effects reflect human capital accumulation, learning about comparative advantage, or within-occupation firm upgrading: “completely ruling out a learning or firms story requires a much richer model” (p. 4281).
Serially correlated unobservable aggregate preference shocks: “identification is difficult in this situation... good instruments will be hard to find in practice” (footnote 23, p. 4279).
Two-way clustering over individuals and time: “Lacking an ideal solution, I present two sets of standard errors” (p. 4280).

estimator.value: Two-stage structural estimator: pseudo-EM (Arcidiacono and Miller 2011) first stage for unobserved types and income parameters, then nonlinear least squares on the finite-dependence estimating equation (17) (objective (18))

estimation.specification: Equation (17)/(18), full model: occupation-specific human capital (tenure), occupations and sectors, demographic controls
controls: age and age squared in the cost shifter f(omega) (equation (9))
occupation-triple task-distance terms in log C(o, o') (equation (10))
sector-switch and occupation-switch indicators (Gamma^S, Gamma^O) in log C(o, o')
estimation.clustering: No clustering; two sets of block-bootstrapped standard errors — blocks by individual history (parentheses, re-estimating both stages) and blocks over time periods in the second stage (brackets).

adjustment_set.label: occupational task distance between o and o'

heterogeneity.dimension: occupational tenure / human capital (column (1) versus columns (2)-(5))
heterogeneity.finding: “The estimates of 1/rho ignoring human capital, even accounting for occupations, are around two-fifths of the point estimation in the main specification” (p. 4286).

heterogeneity.dimension: type of move (within-sector occupation switch versus sector switch)
heterogeneity.finding: Table 6: switching across occupations requires 4.2 years of income while across sectors requires only 2.5 (p. 4287).

ambiguities: Table 5 prints no stars, p-values or confidence intervals. statistically_significant is inferred from the ratio of the printed estimate to the printed block-bootstrap standard error (evidence e8).

Two standard errors are printed for column (1): (0.045) blocking by individual and [0.104] blocking over time periods. se_or_ci keeps both verbatim; the parsed `se` field carries the parenthesised individual-block value, which is the one the table reports first.

evidence.how: Table 5 reports no number of observations for any column; no N is printed anywhere for the second-stage regression.
Table 5 reports no p-values, no confidence intervals and no significance stars; only two sets of block-bootstrapped standard errors.
Neither Table 5 nor its note reports a baseline/control-group mean or a standard deviation of the dependent variable (the log relative transition rate).
Significance is not starred in Table 5; it is inferred from the ratio of the printed point estimate to the printed block-bootstrap standard error (|1.428| / 0.045 = 31.73).

value.as_printed: log[pi_t(omega, o, o')/pi_t(omega, o, o)] + beta log[pi_{t+1}(omega', o', o'')/pi_{t+1}(omega'', o, o'')] = -f(omega)C(o, o')/rho + (eta_{o'} - eta_o)/rho - beta[f(omega')C(o', o'') - f(omega)C(o, o')]/rho + (1/rho)(w_{o't} E_varsigma H_{o'}(omega, varsigma) - w_{ot} E_varsigma H_o(omega, varsigma)) + zeta_{oo'o''t} + m_{oo'o''t}
value.lhs: log[pi_t(omega, o, o')/pi_t(omega, o, o)] + beta log[pi_{t+1}(omega', o', o'')/pi_{t+1}(omega'', o, o'')]

terms.expression: (1/rho)(w_{o't} E_varsigma H_{o'}(omega, varsigma) - w_{ot} E_varsigma H_o(omega, varsigma))

index_sets.over: occupation-triples: 38 author-defined occupation-sector pairs plus non-employment states
worker states: observed age grid, skill group, occupational tenure, and unobserved type k = 1..6

value.normalisation: Discount factor fixed at beta = 0.96 (p. 4276). log(theta) for type 6 (college-educated, high absolute advantage) normalised to 0 in every occupation (p. 4282). The value of non-employment for 23-year-old, high absolute advantage, college-educated workers normalised to 0 (p. 4287). Costs C(o, o') are normalised by the income of the source occupation (Table 6 note, p. 4285). Staying in o (the o, o, o' arc) is the differenced-out reference career arc.

value.claimed_domain: Dynamic adjustment models of labour reallocation generally, not only the Danish application: the author argues that the sensitivity of the switching elasticity to occupational tenure “should give pause to how we interpret the increasing number of dynamic adjustment models ignoring this feature of the data”.
boundary_conditions: Denmark and the United States have different institutions, workers and geography, so the comparison of methods across countries is speculative (footnote 34, p. 4285).
“Without US data, it is impossible to know how human capital changes estimates in the United States” (footnote 34, p. 4285).

theory_referenced: Dynamic discrete choice with conditional choice probabilities (Hotz and Miller 1993; Arcidiacono and Miller 2011; Scott 2014)
Artuç, Chaudhuri, and McLaren (2010) dynamic model of labour reallocation and trade
Occupation-specific human capital (Shaw 1987; Kambourov and Manovskii 2009b)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: He estimates ​1/ρ​ at 2.2, which is close to my estimate.
Highlighting these connections is useful as ACM has become a standard model for reallocation in the trade literature, and will serve as a benchmark for understanding quantitative results.
Moreover, there are other methods, such as the full solution method of Dix-Carneiro (2014), that can capture human capital differences across workers, but cannot allow for large choice sets.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Monte Carlo simulations on a simplified version of the model assessing short-sample bias: “available upon request” (footnote 26, p. 4280).

anchor_quote.text: This parameter is one of the most important in the model, as it governs the elasticity of switching occupations with respect to income shocks.

links.pointer_quote: I show that ignoring human capital biases estimates of adjustment costs upward by a factor of 3.

claims.statement: In column (1): full model with specific human capital, occupations and demographic controls, the estimated mean switching cost scaled by rho (mean C/rho) is 4.618.

treatment.label: Switching occupation-triple (moving from occupation-sector state o to a different state o')

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research): worker income and occupation, measured each November, linked to firms via the Firm Accounting Statistics Register (FIRE) for the sector dimension. No Statistics Denmark variable codes are printed.

definition.value: A change of occupation-triple between consecutive Novembers. The cost it carries enters equation (17) as -f(omega)C(o, o')/rho, where f(omega) = exp{alpha_1 age + alpha_2 age^2 + alpha_3 1{skill = med} + alpha_4 1{skill = high} + theta_f} (equation (9)) and log C(o, o') is parameterised in occupational task space (equation (10)).

timing.value: Measured between consecutive Novembers, t and t+1, over 1996-2008; the worker's state omega is measured at the beginning of period t, before the choice.

outcome.label: Mean switching cost scaled by the dispersion of the idiosyncratic cost shocks, C/rho

register_source.value: IDA: occupation (ISCO two-digit) and employment status each November, linked to FIRE for the NACE 1.1 industry/sector. No Statistics Denmark variable codes are printed.

definition.value: Table 5 row “Mean C/rho”: the simple mean across all cells of the estimated cost matrix C(o, o'), divided by rho, with no adjustment for observed transition rates. Costs C are normalised by the income of the source occupation, so C is expressed in years of source-occupation income.

timing.value: Transition rates between consecutive Novembers t to t+1 and t+1 to t+2, pooled over 1996-2008 (T = 12).

units.value: mean of C/rho across all cells of the cost matrix; C is measured in years of income in the source occupation, so the printed figure is years of income divided by rho

magnitude.interpretation: For column (1), multiplying by rho gives costs of 3.2 years of income, or 17 percent of annual income when annualised; the paper contrasts this with “up to 15 years of income” in column (3) and 59 percent (column 2) and 31 percent (column 5) of annual income when annualised (pp. 4285-4286).

Skill prices w_{ot} and the human capital function H_o(omega, varsigma) (including returns to occupational tenure, age and unobserved comparative advantage theta) come from the first-stage income regression. In columns (2)-(4) the human capital terms are suppressed and incumbent wages are used instead.

timing.value: Measured between consecutive Novembers, t and t+1, over 1996-2008; the worker's state omega is measured at the beginning of period t, before the choice.

timing.value: Transition rates between consecutive Novembers t to t+1 and t+1 to t+2, pooled over 1996-2008 (T = 12).

units.value: coefficient 1/rho: the semi-elasticity of the log relative transition rate with respect to the income differential, in units of years of income (equivalently, the inverse of the scale rho of the Gumbel switching-cost shocks)

two unobserved comparative-advantage types within each skill group (six types)
population.selection: Conditioning on being an employed or non-employed Danish resident aged 24-64 with a non-imputed occupation code and income between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles; immigrants are more likely to be dropped because their education is often missing (footnote 3, p. 4264).

identification.instrument: The IV strategy of Artuç, Chaudhuri, and McLaren (2010); the specific instruments are not named in the main text (“I use exactly ACM’s estimator in each of specifications (2)-(4). Details are in online Appendix E.”, footnote 33, p. 4285)

key_assumptions.assumption: The t+1 forecast errors in the estimating equation are uncorrelated over time and with contemporaneous variables at time t (so the realized transition rate can replace the expectation).
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test. key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix H relaxes the timing assumption in two directions (wage shocks observed; neither wage shocks nor skill prices observed); the author reports “Neither assumption significantly changes my estimates” (p. 4280).

key_assumptions.assumption: Assumption 2 (Conditional Independence and GEV(1) Errors): conditional on the state, the switching-cost shocks are i.i.d. across occupation-triples, individuals and time, Gumbel distributed.

key_assumptions.assumption: The discount factor is not identified and is fixed at beta = 0.96.

threats_discussed: Workers may have more or less information than assumed, making observed equilibrium skill prices a noisy measure of forecasted skill prices; Dickstein and Morales (2018) show measurement error can lead to large and ambiguously signed biases in nonlinear models (p. 4280).

Serially correlated unobservable aggregate preference shocks (shocks to eta) would violate the forecast-error assumption; identification is difficult and good instruments hard to find (footnote 23, p. 4279).

Residuals combine first-stage measurement error in transition probabilities and workers' forecast errors, so one should ideally cluster over both individuals and time, which is infeasible here (p. 4280).
The panel is short (T = 12): few time clusters for the bootstrap and possible small-sample bias (p. 4280).
Tenure effects may reflect learning about comparative advantage or within-occupation firm upgrading rather than human capital accumulation (p. 4281).
robustness_checks: Two sets of block-bootstrapped standard errors: blocks by individual (re-estimating both stages) and blocks over time periods in the second stage (p. 4280).

Online Appendix G: a sqrt(N)-consistent estimator based on Altuğ and Miller (1998); “This changes point-estimates slightly, but 1/rho and the parameters governing costs all remain significant” (p. 4280).

Online Appendix H: alternative timing assumptions (wage shocks observed, as in Dix-Carneiro 2014; and neither wage shocks nor skill prices observed) — “Neither assumption significantly changes my estimates” (p. 4280).
Online Appendix F: an alternative model with sector- as well as occupation-specific human capital (p. 4281).

unresolved_confounders: Whether tenure effects reflect human capital accumulation, learning about comparative advantage, or within-occupation firm upgrading: “completely ruling out a learning or firms story requires a much richer model” (p. 4281).
Serially correlated unobservable aggregate preference shocks: “identification is difficult in this situation... good instruments will be hard to find in practice” (footnote 23, p. 4279).
Two-way clustering over individuals and time: “Lacking an ideal solution, I present two sets of standard errors” (p. 4280).

key_assumptions.assumption: Assumption 1 (Information Sets): the worker knows the full set of skill prices at time t when choosing an occupation-triple; idiosyncratic productivity shocks are unknown at the time decisions are made and revealed only upon employment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix H relaxes the timing assumption in two directions (wage shocks observed; neither wage shocks nor skill prices observed); the author reports “Neither assumption significantly changes my estimates” (p. 4280).

key_assumptions.assumption: Assumption 2 (Conditional Independence and GEV(1) Errors): conditional on the state, the switching-cost shocks are i.i.d. across occupation-triples, individuals and time, Gumbel distributed.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix F estimates an alternative model with sector- as well as occupation-specific human capital; the author reports the magnitudes of the returns to occupational tenure are robust (pp. 4274, 4281).

key_assumptions.assumption: Finite dependence / renewal: two workers who are identical at t-1 and both switch into a new occupation at t+1 are again in the same state at t+2, regardless of any intervening career decision, so the initial and final continuation values difference out.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows from Assumption 4 by construction; no separate empirical test is offered.

formal.as_written: T(T(omega, o, o), o, o') = T(T(omega, o, o'), o', o'')

key_assumptions.assumption: The discount factor is not identified and is fixed at beta = 0.96.

Finite mixture: unobserved comparative advantage theta is drawn at the start of a career from a distribution with finite support, with two unobserved types per skill group (six types in all), and a combination of workers whose collective transitions span the set of occupations identifies the full vector of productivity shifters.

threats_discussed: Workers may have more or less information than assumed, making observed equilibrium skill prices a noisy measure of forecasted skill prices; Dickstein and Morales (2018) show measurement error can lead to large and ambiguously signed biases in nonlinear models (p. 4280).
If human capital is partially transferable, equation (17) is misspecified and both left- and right-hand-side variables carry nonclassical measurement error (p. 4281).

Serially correlated unobservable aggregate preference shocks (shocks to eta) would violate the forecast-error assumption; identification is difficult and good instruments hard to find (footnote 23, p. 4279).

Residuals combine first-stage measurement error in transition probabilities and workers' forecast errors, so one should ideally cluster over both individuals and time, which is infeasible here (p. 4280).
The panel is short (T = 12): few time clusters for the bootstrap and possible small-sample bias (p. 4280).
Tenure effects may reflect learning about comparative advantage or within-occupation firm upgrading rather than human capital accumulation (p. 4281).
robustness_checks: Two sets of block-bootstrapped standard errors: blocks by individual (re-estimating both stages) and blocks over time periods in the second stage (p. 4280).

Online Appendix G: a sqrt(N)-consistent estimator based on Altuğ and Miller (1998); “This changes point-estimates slightly, but 1/rho and the parameters governing costs all remain significant” (p. 4280).
Online Appendix B.9: the split-sample bias correction of Dhaene and Jochmans (2015); “The bias is small, but not insignificant” (p. 4280).

Online Appendix H: alternative timing assumptions (wage shocks observed, as in Dix-Carneiro 2014; and neither wage shocks nor skill prices observed) — “Neither assumption significantly changes my estimates” (p. 4280).
Online Appendix F: an alternative model with sector- as well as occupation-specific human capital (p. 4281).

unresolved_confounders: Whether tenure effects reflect human capital accumulation, learning about comparative advantage, or within-occupation firm upgrading: “completely ruling out a learning or firms story requires a much richer model” (p. 4281).
Serially correlated unobservable aggregate preference shocks: “identification is difficult in this situation... good instruments will be hard to find in practice” (footnote 23, p. 4279).
Two-way clustering over individuals and time: “Lacking an ideal solution, I present two sets of standard errors” (p. 4280).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated labour-supply model of Sections II-III and the demand side calibrated in Table 7 are correctly specified, and the counterfactual is computed by solving that model.
No anticipation: neither young nor old workers can react to import competition before it begins.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix I announces import competition ten periods in advance; in that setting “the differences between young and old workers is more pronounced” (p. 4297).

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual holds technology shocks fixed, so industry TFP does not respond to the import price change; the two simulated economies differ only in the observed changes in import prices from 1996 to 2005.
Foreign prices are exogenous to the Danish labour market: Denmark is a small open economy whose changes in import competition are plausibly exogenous.
The observed 1996 equilibrium is the initial equilibrium, and the new steady state is assumed to be reached at 40 periods.
Changes in the price of energy-related commodities (coke and petroleum) are shut down, to focus on industries associated with offshoring and import competition.
The same idiosyncratic shocks are drawn in the shocked and non-shocked simulations, so the comparison is within-simulated-worker.

threats_discussed: Geography is ignored; “While this may be reasonable for Denmark, it is likely not the case in countries like Germany or the United States” (p. 4299).
Capital reallocation and trade imbalances are not modelled, which could be important along the transition path for workers (p. 4299).
Heterogeneity in reasons for entering non-employment is not modelled and is assumed not to interact with aggregate shocks (footnote 20, p. 4275).
Switching costs are an amalgam of psychic costs, labour market frictions and search costs “with scant normative interpretation”, so only income, not welfare, is reported (p. 4296).
The non-pecuniary benefit and non-employment parameters “are less precisely estimated than others” and the alternative estimator in online Appendix G gives a negative eta (footnote 37, p. 4287).
robustness_checks: Online Appendix Table A.14 reproduces the lifetime-earnings results including non-pecuniary benefits; “the qualitative message remains the same” (p. 4296).
Online Appendix I announces import competition ten periods in advance (p. 4297).
Online Appendix Figure 9 plots the real skill price series and aggregate real income (footnote 46, p. 4294).
Counterfactuals are reported as qualitatively and quantitatively robust to 1/rho in (1.4, 2.2) (footnote 36, p. 4286).
Worker-weighted rather than unweighted sector averages “does not change the qualitative point” (footnote 45, p. 4294).
unresolved_confounders: Whether the estimated fixed switching costs reflect retraining, search frictions or psychic costs: “Further unpacking the black box of switching costs is an important step” (p. 4299).
The role of geography in worker adjustment, which the model abstracts from (p. 4299).
Capital adjustment and trade imbalances along the transition path (p. 4299).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated labour-supply model of Sections II-III and the demand side calibrated in Table 7 are correctly specified, and the counterfactual is computed by solving that model.
No anticipation: neither young nor old workers can react to import competition before it begins.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix I announces import competition ten periods in advance; in that setting “the differences between young and old workers is more pronounced” (p. 4297).

key_assumptions.assumption: The counterfactual holds technology shocks fixed, so industry TFP does not respond to the import price change; the two simulated economies differ only in the observed changes in import prices from 1996 to 2005.
Foreign prices are exogenous to the Danish labour market: Denmark is a small open economy whose changes in import competition are plausibly exogenous.
The observed 1996 equilibrium is the initial equilibrium, and the new steady state is assumed to be reached at 40 periods.
Changes in the price of energy-related commodities (coke and petroleum) are shut down, to focus on industries associated with offshoring and import competition.
The same idiosyncratic shocks are drawn in the shocked and non-shocked simulations, so the comparison is within-simulated-worker.

threats_discussed: Geography is ignored; “While this may be reasonable for Denmark, it is likely not the case in countries like Germany or the United States” (p. 4299).
Capital reallocation and trade imbalances are not modelled, which could be important along the transition path for workers (p. 4299).
Heterogeneity in reasons for entering non-employment is not modelled and is assumed not to interact with aggregate shocks (footnote 20, p. 4275).
Switching costs are an amalgam of psychic costs, labour market frictions and search costs “with scant normative interpretation”, so only income, not welfare, is reported (p. 4296).
The non-pecuniary benefit and non-employment parameters “are less precisely estimated than others” and the alternative estimator in online Appendix G gives a negative eta (footnote 37, p. 4287).
robustness_checks: Online Appendix Table A.14 reproduces the lifetime-earnings results including non-pecuniary benefits; “the qualitative message remains the same” (p. 4296).
Online Appendix I announces import competition ten periods in advance (p. 4297).
Online Appendix Figure 9 plots the real skill price series and aggregate real income (footnote 46, p. 4294).
Counterfactuals are reported as qualitatively and quantitatively robust to 1/rho in (1.4, 2.2) (footnote 36, p. 4286).
Worker-weighted rather than unweighted sector averages “does not change the qualitative point” (footnote 45, p. 4294).
unresolved_confounders: Whether the estimated fixed switching costs reflect retraining, search frictions or psychic costs: “Further unpacking the black box of switching costs is an important step” (p. 4299).
The role of geography in worker adjustment, which the model abstracts from (p. 4299).
Capital adjustment and trade imbalances along the transition path (p. 4299).

identification.source_of_variation: Within-worker persistence of income in a given occupation-triple, used by the EM algorithm to allocate workers to unobserved comparative-advantage types; the comparison is between the first stage with and without those types.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated labour-supply model of Sections II-III and the demand side calibrated in Table 7 are correctly specified, and the counterfactual is computed by solving that model.

The timing assumption implies that an income regression with worker-occupation-triple fixed effects is consistent for the income parameters up to a normalization, and the finite-types assumption lets a set of workers whose transitions span the occupations identify the full vector of productivity shifters.
Tenure effects are interpreted as occupation-specific human capital, not learning about comparative advantage or within-occupation firm upgrading.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The author notes that “many authors suggest the bulk of experimentation happens in youth”, that the sample starts at age 23 and that “nearly 80 percent of occupational switching occurs after age 28” (p. 4281).

threats_discussed: Tenure effects “can also reflect learning (as I treat comparative advantage as known), or within-occupation firm upgrading that generates tenure effects” (p. 4281).
robustness_checks: Online Appendix F shows the magnitudes of the returns to occupational tenure are robust to extending the model to allow for sector-specific capital (p. 4281).
unresolved_confounders: “While completely ruling out a learning or firms story requires a much richer model” (p. 4281).

identification.source_of_variation: The simulated decline in foreign import prices from 1996 to 2005 fed through the calibrated general equilibrium model, compared with a counterfactual holding import prices fixed at base levels.

claims.statement: Between 1995 and 2005 the aggregate index of foreign prices Denmark faces, measured relative to the Danish CPI, declined by 17 percent.

treatment.label: Calendar time, 1995-2005: the rise of China and Eastern Europe as sources of Danish imports

register_source.value: Danish customs data (import transactions, product by partner country) within the Discretionary Foreign Trade Database (UHDI); Danish custom codes mapped to industries using Prodcom. No Statistics Denmark variable codes are printed.

definition.value: The period over which Danish import prices are measured; the aggregate index is normalised to 1 in the initial year and presented relative to the Danish CPI.

outcome.label: Aggregate Danish import price index relative to the Danish CPI

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research): occupation (ISCO two-digit) and income measured each November, linked to firms and their NACE 1.1 industry code via the Firm Accounting Statistics Register (FIRE). No Statistics Denmark variable codes are printed.

definition.value: Industry-level exact/CES import price indices built from Danish customs unit values by the Broda and Weinstein (2006) method, aggregated with import shares (Panel B plots both lagged-year weights and 1996 weights), expressed relative to the Danish CPI.

units.value: percent change in the aggregate import price index between 1995 and 2005, relative to the Danish CPI

magnitude.interpretation: “Over this time period, the rise of China and Eastern Europe led to a 17 percent decline in the aggregate import price index” (p. 4261).

estimand.target_population: Danish merchandise imports, 1995-2005
estimand.time_horizon: change over 1995 to 2005

population.description: Danish customs import transactions, 1995-2005, mapped to 22 industries using the Prodcom concordance.
population.selection: Changes in the price of energy-related commodities (coke and petroleum) are shut down (footnote 44, p. 4292).

identification.source_of_variation: Observed changes in Danish import unit values by product and partner country, 1995-2005, driven by the rise of China and Eastern Europe.

key_assumptions.assumption: A transition is defined as a change from the worker's position when last employed, and transitions into non-employment are excluded.

Occupations are measured by ISCO two-digit codes as recorded by Statistics Denmark and aggregated by the author into 38 occupation-sector pairs; observations whose occupation Statistics Denmark flags as imputed are dropped, and incomes in the top and bottom 2.5 percent are dropped.
The 2005 recoding from NACE 1.1 to NACE 2 does not generate material spurious reallocation; industries are concorded across time.
key_assumptions.supported_by: “The rise in mobility also occurred across occupations, which were unaffected by the code change, suggesting the uptick is genuine” (footnote 11, p. 4266).

threats_discussed: Occupation codes are occasionally imputed by Statistics Denmark from education, industry and income; such observations are dropped to avoid circularity (pp. 4263-4264).
The 2005 recoding from NACE 1.1 to NACE 2 may produce some spurious reallocation (footnote 11, p. 4266).
IDAS contains limited information on immigrants and Danes commuting abroad; immigrants' education is often missing so they are more likely to be dropped (footnote 3, p. 4264).
robustness_checks: Stylized facts shown for various levels of occupational disaggregation (ISCO 2-digit, ISCO 3-digit, author-defined pairs, firms) (p. 4264, Table 1).
Comparisons between sample aggregates and published national accounts in online Appendix D.1 (p. 4263).

ambiguities: The figure caption dates the change 1995-2005 while the counterfactual text refers to “the observed changes in import prices from 1996 to 2005” (p. 4287) and Panel B is indexed from 1996; both datings are the paper's own.
